## Overview

This tutorial is an R adaptation of the ASDC tutorial
[*Examine data details and download TEMPO files using earthaccess*](https://nasa.github.io/ASDC_Data_and_User_Services/TEMPO/how_to_examine_TEMPO_data_using_earthaccess.html)
by Alexander Radkevich (NASA Atmospheric Science Data Center), which uses Python.
Here we use R, with the [earthdatalogin](https://boettiger-lab.github.io/earthdatalogin/)
package for authentication and search.

[TEMPO](https://tempo.si.edu/) (Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution) measures
air pollutants, including nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), over North America. We will search for
Level 3 NO₂ data, read the tropospheric and stratospheric NO₂ columns and the quality flag,
work out which pixels are usable, and map total column NO₂ over the central United States.

- **Purpose:** Show how to find, read, quality-filter and map TEMPO NO₂ data in R.
- **Outcomes:** You will be able to search for TEMPO granules, read variables from a
  grouped netCDF file in the cloud, build quality masks, and plot the result.
- **Process:** Authenticate, search, read, mask, crop, plot.

## Learning objectives

- Authenticate with NASA Earthdata Login using `earthdatalogin`
- Search for granules by collection, time and bounding box
- Read variables from a grouped netCDF-4 file with `terra`, without downloading the whole file
- Apply fill-value and quality-flag masks, and understand why they differ
- Subset to a region and make a map

## Prerequisites

| Concepts | Importance | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [earthdatalogin](https://boettiger-lab.github.io/earthdatalogin/) | Necessary | Authentication and search |
| [Earthdata Login account](https://urs.earthdata.nasa.gov) | Necessary | Free; needed to access TEMPO data |
| Understanding of NetCDF | Helpful | TEMPO files use groups |
| Basic `terra` | Helpful | Raster data in R |

- **Time to learn**: about 30 minutes
- **System requirements**: R with GDAL built with netCDF/HDF5 support (GDAL ≥ 3.4 recommended)

---

## Imports

```{r}
library(earthdatalogin)
library(terra)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyterra)
library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)
```

## Authenticate

`edl_netrc()` configures GDAL and curl so that remote files can be read directly. It uses the
`EARTHDATA_USER` and `EARTHDATA_PASSWORD` environment variables. If those aren't set it falls
back to a shared default login (`rpackage`) rather than reading `~/.netrc`, which quickly gets
rate-limited, so we supply our own credentials.

```{r}
edl_netrc(
  username = Sys.getenv("EARTHDATA_USER"),
  password = Sys.getenv("EARTHDATA_PASSWORD")
)
```

## Search for TEMPO granules

We want the TEMPO Level 3 NO₂ product, version 3 (`TEMPO_NO2_L3`, `V03`), for
1 September 2024 over a region around the centre of the contiguous United States
(38°N, 96°W, plus or minus 5° of latitude and 6° of longitude).

```{r}
lat <- 38.0
lon <- -96.0

# bounding_box is a single string: "west,south,east,north"
bbox <- paste(lon - 6, lat - 5, lon + 6, lat + 5, sep = ",")

results <- edl_search(
  short_name = "TEMPO_NO2_L3",
  version = "V03",
  temporal = c("2024-09-01T00:00:00Z", "2024-09-01T23:59:59Z"),
  bounding_box = bbox,
  parse_results = FALSE
)

length(results)
```

The search returns 18 granules, the same as the Python tutorial. Note that times are UTC, so the
first granule (scan 16) was acquired at 23:58 UTC on 31 August.

### Look at the results

`edl_extract_urls()` pulls the data links out of the search results. File names follow the
pattern `TEMPO_NO2_L3_V03_<timestamp>_S0xx.nc`, where `S0xx` is the scan number.

```{r}
urls <- edl_extract_urls(results)

granules <- data.frame(
  file = basename(urls),
  scan = sub(".*_(S[0-9]+)\\.nc$", "\\1", basename(urls)),
  time = as.POSIXct(
    sub(".*_V03_([0-9]{8}T[0-9]{6})Z_.*", "\\1", basename(urls)),
    format = "%Y%m%dT%H%M%S", tz = "UTC"
  ),
  url = urls
)

granules[, c("file", "scan", "time")]
```

## Open a granule

Each TEMPO L3 file is large (about 890 MB for this one). Rather than downloading it, we open it remotely with
GDAL's `/vsicurl/` handler, which reads only the parts of the file we ask for.

We will use the granule from 15:38 UTC (scan 7), the same one as the original tutorial.

```{r}
url <- granules$url[grepl("20240901T153815Z_S007", granules$url)]
nc <- paste0("/vsicurl/", url)
```

TEMPO files are organized in netCDF *groups*. The data variables are in the `product`
group, while latitude and longitude are at the root. Let's list what GDAL sees:

```{r}
describe(nc, sds = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-note}
TODO: Verify how GDAL names the group variables on the Hub (e.g.
`NETCDF:"...":/product/vertical_column_troposphere`). If `terra` cannot open the group
variables or georeference them, switch to the hybrid approach: read with
`stars::read_mdim()` and convert with `terra::rast()` (see PLAN.md, section 4).
:::

## Read the variables

We need three variables from the `product` group:

- `vertical_column_troposphere`: tropospheric NO₂ column
- `vertical_column_stratosphere`: stratospheric NO₂ column
- `main_data_quality_flag`: quality flag (0 is good)

```{r}
read_tempo <- function(nc, var) {
  rast(sprintf('NETCDF:"%s":/product/%s', nc, var))
}

trop  <- read_tempo(nc, "vertical_column_troposphere")
strat <- read_tempo(nc, "vertical_column_stratosphere")
qf    <- read_tempo(nc, "main_data_quality_flag")

trop
```

```{r}
units(trop)       # expect molecules/cm^2
dim(trop)         # expect 2950 rows x 7750 columns x 1 layer
```

## Find the good pixels

Not every pixel has a usable value. There are two things to check:

1. **Fill values.** Missing pixels hold a fill value (-1e30) rather than `NA`.
2. **The quality flag.** `main_data_quality_flag == 0` marks good retrievals.

These do not select the same pixels, so they need to be combined.

```{r}
fv_trop  <- -1e30
fv_strat <- -1e30

# terra normally converts the netCDF _FillValue to NA for us; check that this happened
global(trop, "min", na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r}
# TODO: confirm the fill value is read as NA by terra; if it is, the `!= fv`
# comparisons in the original tutorial become `!is.na()`.
not_fill <- !is.na(trop) & !is.na(strat)
good <- (qf == 0) & not_fill
best <- good & (trop > 0) & (strat > 0)

counts <- data.frame(
  criterion = c("Not fill value", "Quality flag = 0", "Good (QF = 0 and not fill)",
                "Best (good and both columns > 0)"),
  pixels = c(
    global(not_fill, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]],
    global(qf == 0, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]],
    global(good, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]],
    global(best, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]
  )
)
counts
```

::: {.callout-note}
For this granule the Python tutorial reports 22,862,500 non-fill pixels, 7,363,629 with
a quality flag of 0 and 6,262,529 "best" pixels. These are a useful check that the R
version is doing the same thing. TODO: compare.
:::

Some "good" pixels still have negative NO₂ columns, which are not physically meaningful.
These arise from noise in the retrieval, so the "best" mask additionally drops them. This
is a simple heuristic, not an official quality criterion.

## Subset to the region of interest

```{r}
roi <- ext(lon - 6, lon + 6, lat - 5, lat + 5)

trop_roi  <- crop(trop, roi)
strat_roi <- crop(strat, roi)
best_roi  <- crop(best, roi)

total_roi <- (trop_roi + strat_roi) |> mask(best_roi, maskvalues = 0)
```

## Map total column NO₂

```{r}
states <- ne_states(country = "United States of America", returnclass = "sf")

ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = total_roi) +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = NA, colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.2, linetype = "dotted") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    na.value = "transparent",
    limits = c(0, 5e16),
    oob = scales::squish,
    name = "Total NO₂ column\n(molecules/cm²)"
  ) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(lon - 6, lon + 6), ylim = c(lat - 5, lat + 5), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
